description: 319 pages : 24 cm

results.description: The Ballad Years was a twelve-part encyclopaedia-style series written by Don Wicks and first published via In Tune International , a subscription-only magazine focused on popular music from around 1936 to 1960. The Ballad Years spans roughly the same era - in Don's words, it is "a comprehensive encyclopaedia of British popular music performers, spanning the period from the war years to the early sixties." It includes biographies of notable performers with a singles discography for each artist. There are also entries for a few related subjects. The original printed books sold out, but Don kept the files updated: for example, when a performer died. These updated versions were available as a data CD from Don directly, in ten parts, plus five galleries, a contents listing and introduction. There are therefore 17 files in total. The book was not made widely available via a commercial publisher, so the files are here as free downloads. They are being uploaded ten years to the day since his passing, with permission from his family. The files are the last versions he edited in 2012. Grateful thanks for Tony Bradley for making the updated files available to me. The Ballad Years is an essential resource for anyone interested in British popular music of the post-war years, covering the late 1940s, the 1950s, and early 1960s. Many of these artists have not been written about elsewhere, and information on them is hard to come by. The listing of their singles is also data which has been lost to the mists of time in the digital era. May 2026 update: two files have been added. One is an Excel spreadsheet with an artist index, featuring real names, dates of birth and dates of death, where known. This covers solo performers and selected group members (such as those with more static line-ups). The “mystery artists” Word document lists artists who are missing the above information. If you can help, please get in touch via the email address in the document’s Comments. About the author Donald Stanley Wicks was born on 10 March 1938 in Bristol, Gloucestershire, England. He left school at 15, becoming a painter and decorator. He married Janet Burbidge in Bristol in 1960, and the couple had two children, Kevin and Sarah. Later, after marrying, Don joined the Dock police, and after three years, transferred to the fire brigade, where he stayed until his retirement. He was active in charity fundraising. His hobbies, as well as avid music appreciation, were photography, and, after his children had grown up, travelling the UK with Janet in various campervans. Don Wicks died on 5 February 2013 in Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, England, aged 74. He was survived by his wife, Janet, and children, Kevin and Sarah. results.title: ERIC EJ1057153: Revolutionizing the Use of Natural History Collections in Education
results.creator: ERIC
results.description: Natural history collections are an irreplaceable and extensive record of life, and form the basis of our understanding of biodiversity on our planet. Broad-scale educational accessibility to these vast specimen collections, specimen images, and their associated data is currently severely hampered. With emerging technologies and massive efforts towards digitizing specimens, there is enormous potential to revolutionize biology education at all levels. These specimens, images, and data provide an unparalleled opportunity to integrate both inquiry-based and place-based learning into education at all levels and in all venues. Natural history specimens and associated data have an inherent focus on spatial and temporal variation and are uniquely situated to integrate traditionally segregated disciplines, and to develop creativity, generative thinking, and rigorous inquiry; qualities that will be required of successful future generations. These collections are excellent tools for engaging students in biology and helping students draw connections among sub-disciplines within biology (e.g., ecology, evolution, and molecular genetics) and connect biology to other fields (e.g., art, computer science, and geography). Natural history specimens can nurture student interest in solving important societal issues such as sustainability, invasive species, declining biodiversity, food security, climate change, and emerging pathogens. To realize these educational opportunities we need to overcome the disconnect between educators and museum scientists by providing greater access to teaching collections and building student-friendly digital interfaces and educational modules that demonstrate how to explore the vast natural history collections. There are a growing number of excellent models for overcoming these hurdles that illustrate how these approaches could be expanded and more widely adopted in educational settings/environments.

results.title: Working on screen : representations of the working class in Canadian cinema
description: 1 online resource (xiv, 293 pages)

As themes in film studies literature, work and the working class have long occupied a peripheral place in the evaluation of Canadian cinema, often set aside in the critical literature for the sake of a unifying narrative that assumes a division between Québécois and English Canada's film production, a social-realist documentary aesthetic, and what might be called a 'younger brother' relationship with the United States. In Working on Screen, contributors examine representations of socio-economic class across the spectrum of Canadian film, video, and television, covering a wide range of class-related topics and dealing with them as they intersect with history, political activism, globalization, feminism, queer rights, masculinity, regional marginalization, cinematic realism, and Canadian nationalism. Of concern in this collection are the daily lives and struggles of working people and the ways in which the representation of the experience of class in film fosters or marginalizes a progressive engagement with history, politics, and societies around the world. Working on Screen thus expands the scholarly debates on the concept of national cinema and builds on the rich, formative efforts of Canadian cultural criticism that held dear the need for cultural autonomy

results.description: Rail Travel News, [note:  earliest issues, #001 through #098, were published under the name "Rail Travel Newsletter"], independent periodical journal published from late 1970 until mid-2004.  It covered the end of the era of passenger trains run by individual U.S. railroad corporations, and the advent of Amtrak, the government-sponsored national system which began operating in mid-1971.  Various issues in this collection, as available to date, approx. half the full press run.  Collection is complete from issue #1 to #308, at the end of 1984 (Vol. 14), and spotty after that, but it does include the final issue, #662.  Publication schedule was theoretically approx. every 2 weeks but it varied.  Pub. covered passenger trains & services primarily in the U.S. but also had articles re:  Canadian & European services as well.  There is a database of the contents, by issue and page, as well as a more detailed "Introduction" article which will tell you more about the history of the publication and this preservation project.  RTN (as it was often called) was alway printed rather inexpensively, so the quality of th text and (esp.) images varied widely.  Description updated:  2022-09-03
